caption:
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney says Claude blocked his set theory work and accused him of distillation, using one AI to train another.
He called it "garbage" after 1 to 2 hours a day of prompting on a company account.
Later he said the anti-distillation feature is the problem, and Claude's top models are "quite excellent overall."

Should AI companies be allowed to cut off paying users like this?

paragraphs.text: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney said on November 25, 2026 that Anthropic's Claude blocked set theory work he was doing and accused him of distillation, the practice of using one AI model's outputs to train another. He made the complaint in a post on X, according to TweakTown and WindowsForum.

In the post, as quoted by TweakTown, Sweeney called Claude "garbage" and said the block came after one to two hours a day of prompting on a company account. He ended by saying Anthropic cannot keep sabotaging customers' work in this way.
What Sweeney did and did not say

The reports describe the result, not the mechanics. According to WindowsForum, Sweeney did not say which Claude model he was using, what his prompts were, or whether he hit a single refusal, a slowdown or a full lockout. None of the coverage quotes the message Claude showed him.

Later the same day, Sweeney narrowed his criticism in a reply on X to coverage of his post. WindowsForum reported that he called the anti-distillation feature itself garbage while describing Claude's leading models as quite excellent overall. SSBCrack News also reported that he clarified the complaint was aimed at the feature rather than at Claude as a whole.
Anthropic had not responded publicly by the evening of November 25, WindowsForum reported.

Distillation lets a company train a cheaper model on the answers of a stronger one, which is why AI labs try to detect accounts that pull large volumes of structured output. WindowsForum, citing Anthropic's own published reporting, wrote that the company says its defenses have cut distillation campaigns sharply and that it puts its false positive rate below 0.1%.

Sweeney's case shows the cost of that trade. A filter tuned to catch bulk extraction can also catch a heavy, legitimate user whose work looks structured and repetitive, such as long sessions on formal mathematics. When the person flagged runs a company that builds on Claude, a rare false positive becomes a public one.
An awkward moment for Epic and Anthropic

The dispute lands while Epic leans further into AI. TweakTown noted that Epic has connected Claude and Gemini to Unreal Engine through the Model Context Protocol, and that the company has argued against mandatory AI disclosure labels on game stores while calling AI an accelerant for real creators.

WindowsForum reported that Epic's Unreal Engine 6 plans include the same Claude and Gemini integration and lean on AI tools to move projects off Blueprints, the visual scripting system many Unreal developers use today.

That makes Sweeney an unusual critic. He is not rejecting AI tools or Claude itself, and his follow up praised the models. His complaint is narrower: that an automated safeguard treated a paying business customer as a suspected copier with no clear explanation. Enterprise customers are likely to ask the same question if similar blocks reach their own teams.

Watch whether Anthropic responds to Sweeney directly or explains how customers can appeal an anti-distillation block, since a clear appeal path would matter most to companies that run long, structured sessions on Claude every day.
